name: Cabernet Sauvignon
intro: Cabernet Sauvignon is a full-bodied red with a reputation for structure. It is widely planted, including in Temecula, and it rarely tastes shy.
aromas: Blackcurrant, black cherry, cedar, and sometimes a green or herbal note when the grapes are less ripe. Warmer sites often show riper, darker fruit.
variations: Bordeaux Cabernet is often blended and can feel firmer and more savory. Napa and other warm regions may show riper fruit and more obvious oak. A cool year and a hot year of the same vineyard can differ. Producer, vintage, and oak are not footnotes.
pairings: Grilled mushrooms, hearty vegetables, lamb, and steak. Protein and a little fat soften the tannin.
serving: A little cooler than a warm room, often about 60 to 65°F. If it tastes dull and hot, cool it for ten minutes and taste again.
fact: Cabernet Sauvignon is a child of Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc. The crossing is old. The confidence is newer.

name: Pinot Noir
intro: Pinot Noir often prefers finesse to force. It can be delicate, earthy, or surprisingly rich, depending on where it grew.
aromas: Cherry, raspberry, sometimes rose, mushroom, or a savory earth note. Oak, when used, should not bury the fruit.
variations: Cooler climates, including much of Burgundy and coastal California, tend toward perfume and freshness. Warmer sites can make a deeper, riper Pinot. Thin skins mean the color and tannin are usually lighter than Cabernet. That is character, not a flaw.
pairings: Roast chicken, mushrooms, salmon, and dishes that do not need a heavy red to stand up.
serving: Cooler than a big red, often about 55 to 60°F. A hot glass makes it taste jammy and tired.
fact: Pinot Noir is genetically unstable, which is one reason so many vineyards talk about clones. Small differences in the vine can show in the glass.

name: Merlot
intro: Merlot is often softer in tannin than Cabernet, which made it easy to underestimate. At its best it is plush, not simple.
aromas: Plum, black cherry, cocoa, and sometimes herbs or cedar. Overripe examples can taste jammy. Careful ones taste rounded.
variations: On Bordeaux’s Right Bank, Merlot often leads the blend and can be serious and long-lived. Elsewhere it may be made for early drinking. Oak and ripeness change it as much as the grape name does.
pairings: Roast poultry, mushrooms, burgers, and tomato dishes that are not fiercely acidic.
serving: About 60 to 65°F. A short time in the glass is usually enough.
fact: Merlot is a parent of Carménère, Malbec, and Cabernet Sauvignon’s sibling family of Bordeaux grapes. It gets around.

name: Syrah / Shiraz
intro: Syrah and Shiraz are the same grape. The name on the label is a hint about style, not a different species.
aromas: Blackberry, black pepper, smoked meat, olive, and violet in cooler examples. Warmer Shiraz may show riper fruit, chocolate, and sweeter oak spice.
variations: Northern Rhône Syrah is often peppery and savory. Australian Shiraz from warm regions is often riper and more generous. Temecula and other warm valleys can land in between. Ask which style is in the glass.
pairings: Grilled foods, lamb, hard cheese, and dishes with a little char or spice that is not extremely hot.
serving: About 60 to 65°F. Peppery Syrah can taste harsh if it is too warm.
fact: Shiraz is the name that traveled with the grape to Australia. Syrah is the name more common in France and in much of California. Same grape.

name: Zinfandel
intro: Zinfandel is a California classic with a wide range, from hearty reds to pale pink wines that are a different style entirely.
aromas: Raspberry, blackberry, briar, and sometimes pepper or jam. Very ripe bottles can taste of raisins. That is a style, and not everyone wants it.
variations: Old-vine red Zinfandel can be concentrated. White Zinfandel is a sweeter pink style made from the same grape, and it should not be judged as a failed red. The grape is the same as Italy’s Primitivo.
pairings: Barbecue, pizza, burgers, and dishes with a little sweetness or char. For a very ripe Zin, food with some fat or a tangy sauce helps.
serving: About 60 to 65°F for the red. Chill a pink one.
fact: DNA work tied Zinfandel to Crljenak Kaštelanski on the Croatian coast, and to Primitivo in Puglia. The family reunion took a while.

name: Malbec
intro: Malbec is best known now from Argentina, though it began in France and still grows there. It often tastes dark, floral, and generous.
aromas: Plum, blackberry, violet, and sometimes cocoa. High-altitude bottles can feel fresher. Very ripe ones can feel plush and oaky.
variations: Cahors in France has a firmer, more rustic tradition. Mendoza made Malbec famous for ripe fruit and violet. Oak and altitude move the style as much as the grape does.
pairings: Grilled beef, mushrooms, and hard cheeses. A fresher bottle can also sit with roasted vegetables.
serving: About 60 to 65°F. Give a tight young bottle a few minutes in the glass.
fact: Malbec is one of the historic Bordeaux varieties, even though Argentina is where most people meet it now.

name: Sangiovese
intro: Sangiovese is the red grape at the heart of Chianti and much of Tuscany. It usually leads with acidity and savory cherry, not with sheer weight.
aromas: Sour cherry, dried herbs, tomato leaf, and sometimes tea or leather with age. Oak can add spice, and too much of it can cover the grape.
variations: Chianti, Brunello, and a California or Temecula Sangiovese are related, not identical. Warmer sites make riper fruit. The high acidity is the family trait to listen for.
pairings: Tomato sauces, pizza, grilled vegetables, and Italian-leaning plates. The acidity is why it likes tomatoes.
serving: About 60 to 65°F. Too warm, and the alcohol steps in front of the cherry.
fact: The name is often linked to the Latin for the blood of Jove. The grape does not require the mythology. The acidity is enough.

name: Tempranillo
intro: Tempranillo is the signature red of Rioja and Ribera del Duero, and it is also grown in Temecula. It can be fresh and fruity or savory and oak-spiced.
aromas: Cherry, plum, dill or coconut when American oak is used, and leather or tobacco with age. Not every bottle tastes of oak. Some are made to show the fruit.
variations: Traditional Rioja often uses American oak and can taste of dill, vanilla, and coconut. Other regions, and many modern bottles, use less oak or French oak and taste fruitier. The grape is early-ripening. The name says so.
pairings: Roasted meats, Manchego and other firm cheeses, mushrooms, and grilled vegetables.
serving: About 60 to 65°F. An older, savory bottle does not need to be icy or hot.
fact: Tempranillo means “a little early.” It ripens before many other red grapes, which is useful in places with a short warm season.

name: Chardonnay
intro: Chardonnay is a shape-shifter. The same grape can taste of green apple and steel, or of peach, butter, and toast.
tannin: Low. White wines are not usually tannic.
aromas: Citrus, apple, and pear when cool and unoaked. Ripe peach, butter, vanilla, and toast when the fruit is riper and the winemaking uses malolactic fermentation or new oak.
variations: Chablis is a famous cool, usually unoaked style. Many California bottles are riper, and some are openly oaky. A label that says unoaked is telling you something useful. Climate, lees stirring, and barrels do the rest.
pairings: Roast chicken, mushrooms, and creamy dishes for a richer bottle. Shellfish and green salads for a crisp one. Match the style, not just the name.
serving: Crisp versions colder, about 45 to 50°F. Richer ones a little warmer so they are not mute.
fact: The buttery note many people associate with Chardonnay usually comes from malolactic fermentation, a bacterial conversion of sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid. It is a choice.

name: Sauvignon Blanc
intro: Sauvignon Blanc is often bright, herbal, and impatient in the best way. It tends to taste vivid rather than creamy.
aromas: Lime, grapefruit, cut grass, green herbs, and, in riper climates, passion fruit or melon. A struck-match or flint note appears in some Loire and oak-influenced bottles.
variations: Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé are classic cooler styles. Marlborough, New Zealand, made the pungent passion-fruit style famous. Warm regions, including parts of California, can be riper and rounder. Oak is less common than in Chardonnay, but it exists.
pairings: Goat cheese, herbs, asparagus if you like that combination, salads, and seafood that is not swimming in cream.
serving: Cold, about 45 to 50°F, but not frozen. Ice hides the herbs.
fact: Sauvignon Blanc is a parent of Cabernet Sauvignon. The family resemblance is easier to see in a herbal note than in the color.

name: Riesling
intro: Riesling can be bone dry or richly sweet. The grape is known for perfume, acidity, and a transparency to place.
aromas: Lime, green apple, white flowers, and sometimes petrol or honey with age. Sweetness, when present, should be held up by acidity, not sitting alone.
variations: Germany uses specific words for ripeness and style. Alsace and Australia have their own traditions. A dry Riesling and a late-harvest Riesling share a grape and little else at the table. Read the label for sweetness if you can. If you cannot, taste.
pairings: Spicy food, pork, salads, and fruit-based dishes. A little sweetness can calm heat. A dry one likes fish and fresh cheeses.
serving: Well chilled, about 45 to 50°F. Sweet versions still need acidity, not just cold.
fact: Riesling’s high acidity is why sweet versions can taste lively instead of cloying. Sugar without acid is soda. Sugar with acid can be wine.

name: Pinot Grigio / Pinot Gris
intro: Pinot Grigio and Pinot Gris are the same grape. The Italian name often signals a lighter, crisper bottle. The French name often signals something richer.
aromas: Pear, lemon, green apple, and sometimes white flowers. Richer Pinot Gris can show ripe pear, honey, and a little spice.
variations: A simple Pinot Grigio is meant to be fresh and easy. Alsace Pinot Gris can be textured and substantial. The grape has pinkish skins, which is why a ramato, or copper-tinged, style exists. Color is a clue, not a grade.
pairings: Light seafood, salads, mild cheeses, and weeknight plates that do not need a loud wine.
serving: Cold, about 45 to 50°F. A richer Pinot Gris can come up a few degrees.
fact: Pinot Gris is a color mutation of Pinot Noir. The family is the same. The glass is not.

name: Chenin Blanc
intro: Chenin Blanc is one of the great under-explained grapes. It can be dry and snapping, or sweet and long-lived, and the acidity is usually the spine.
aromas: Quince, apple, chamomile, honey, and sometimes a woolly or waxy note that sounds odd and tastes distinctive.
variations: The Loire makes dry, sparkling, and sweet Chenin. South Africa has a long tradition of it, sometimes under the old name Steen. Oak and sweetness are choices. High acidity is the thread.
pairings: Roast pork, goat cheese, spicy dishes, and fruit desserts if the wine is sweet. Dry Chenin likes herbs and poultry.
serving: Cool, about 48 to 52°F. Sweet Chenin still wants to be cold enough to taste fresh.
fact: Vouvray, Savennières, and many South African bottlings can all be Chenin Blanc and still argue with one another. That range is the grape’s talent.

name: Gewürztraminer
intro: Gewürztraminer is perfumed and unmistakable when it is typical. The name refers to spice. The glass often smells of lychee and rose.
aromas: Lychee, rose, ginger, and ripe tropical fruit. It can be dry or sweet. The perfume is not a sign that it must be sweet.
variations: Alsace is the reference for many drinkers. Other regions, including cooler corners of the New World, make fresher versions. Lower acidity means a warm, alcoholic bottle can feel heavy. A careful one feels exotic, not tiring.
pairings: Spicy food, stinky washed-rind cheeses, and dishes with ginger or a little sweetness. It is a poor match for a delicate piece of plain fish.
serving: Cold, about 45 to 50°F, so the perfume stays fresh.
fact: Gewürz means spice in German. The umlaut matters to the name. The lychee aroma matters more to the glass.

name: Rosé
intro: Rosé is a way of making wine, not a lesser red and not a single flavor. The color usually comes from a short time on red-grape skins.
tannin: Low, though deeper styles can have a little
aromas: Strawberry, citrus, watermelon, herbs, or, in deeper styles, cherry and a savory note. Pale color does not automatically mean better or worse.
variations: Provence made a pale, dry style famous. Other regions use different grapes and leave the juice on the skins longer. Champagne rosé is often a blend of still red wine into a white base. Sweet pink wines, including many White Zinfandels, are a different category. Read for dryness if it matters to you.
pairings: Salads, seafood, picnic food, and anything you would eat outside. A deeper rosé can take grilled vegetables or charcuterie.
fact: Most rosé gets its color from limited skin contact. Blending red and white is less common, and in much of Europe it is restricted, with Champagne as a famous exception.

name: Sparkling wine
intro: Sparkling wine is wine with bubbles from fermentation under pressure. Champagne is one famous region. It is not the name of every bottle that sparkles.
body: Light to full, depending on style
tannin: Low, unless red grapes and skin contact add a little
aromas: Citrus, apple, bread dough, toast, and sometimes red fruit in rosé. Sweetness ranges from very dry to frankly sweet. Brut is relatively dry.
variations: The traditional method ferments a second time in the bottle and often tastes of bread and toast. The tank method, used for many Proseccos, tends to keep fruitier, fresher aromas. Cava, Crémant, and domestic sparkling are not imitations that failed to be Champagne. They are their own wines.
pairings: Fried foods, salty snacks, shellfish, and the start of a meal. Bubbles and acidity cut richness. Sparkling wine is also happy with no food and no occasion.
serving: Cold, about 40 to 50°F, in a glass that lets you smell it. A flute keeps bubbles. A wider glass shows more aroma. Both are allowed.
fact: The bubbles are carbon dioxide from fermentation, trapped by a closed tank or a corked bottle. They are not added with a soda siphon in traditional sparkling wine.

name: Port and other fortified wines
intro: Fortified wines have a spirit added during or after fermentation. That raises the alcohol and, depending on the timing, can leave sweetness. Port is the famous one. It is not the only one.
acidity: Varies. Madeira is notably acidic. Some sweet wines feel lower in acid.
tannin: Ruby and vintage Ports can be tannic. Many sherries are not.
aromas: Port often shows dark fruit, spice, and, with age, nuts and dried fruit. Fino sherry can smell of almonds and salt. Madeira can smell of caramel and citrus peel. These are families, not one flavor.
variations: Port comes from the Douro in Portugal. Sherry comes from around Jerez in Spain. Madeira comes from its island. Vermouth is aromatized as well as fortified. A dry fino and a vintage Port do not belong in the same sentence at dinner, except to say they are both fortified.
pairings: Sweet Port with blue cheese or chocolate. Dry sherry with salted almonds, olives, or soup. Do not assume every fortified wine wants dessert.
serving: Serve most sweet fortified wines slightly cool, not hot. Serve fino and manzanilla sherry cold, and do not keep an open bottle for weeks. They fade.
fact: If the spirit is added before fermentation finishes, yeast stop, and sugar remains. That is why many Ports are sweet and strong. Timing is the trick.
